notes.front: What does a net control station do?
notes.back: It calls the net to order and directs communications between the stations checking in.
notes.explanation: A net is an organised on-air meeting of stations; the net control station keeps it orderly.
notes.example: At a weekly club net, the net control station opens the net, takes check-ins and gives each station its turn.

notes.front: In net operation, what does “traffic” mean?
notes.back: Formal messages exchanged by net stations.
notes.explanation: Handling traffic accurately is a core public-service skill; the parts of a formal message have names.
notes.example: A formal message handed to the net for delivery, rather than casual conversation.

notes.front: What does the preamble of a formal traffic message contain?
notes.back: The information needed to track the message.
notes.explanation: It lets every station that handles the message keep track of it.
notes.example: Like the tracking details on a parcel, rather than the parcel’s contents or its delivery address.

notes.front: What does “check” mean in a radiogram header?
notes.back: The number of words or word equivalents in the text portion of the message.
notes.explanation: It gives the receiving station a count to compare the copied text against.
notes.example: A message whose text is ten words long carries a check of 10.

notes.front: What is ARES (the Amateur Radio Emergency Service)?
notes.back: A group of licensed amateurs who have voluntarily registered their qualifications and equipment for communications duty in the public service.
notes.explanation: Unlike RACES, it needs no civil defense certification.
notes.example: A local ham who has registered their skills and radios with ARES so they can be called on when help is needed.

notes.front: What is Winlink?
notes.back: A system that relays messages using email addresses based on amateur call signs.
notes.explanation: It lets stations send email-style messages over amateur radio; the pool lists it under public service.
notes.example: A message addressed to an email address built from a ham’s call sign, relayed by radio.

notes.front: When do the FCC Part 97 rules NOT apply to an amateur station?
notes.back: Never: FCC rules always apply, including during RACES, ARES or other emergency operation.
notes.explanation: The pool keys “FCC rules always apply”; 97.103(a) makes the station licensee responsible for operating the station in accordance with the FCC Rules, and RACES is itself a Part 97 service (97.3(a)(38)).
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T2C01; 47 CFR 97.103(a), 97.3(a)(38) (eCFR, current to 2026-09-22)

notes.front: In a net, when should you transmit?
notes.back: Only when directed by the net control station, unless you are reporting an emergency.
notes.explanation: This is the standard net practice the pool keys; it keeps the net orderly.

notes.front: How do you make sure unusual words in a voice message are received correctly?
notes.back: Spell them using a standard phonetic alphabet.
notes.explanation: Phonetics are also encouraged for station identification (97.119(b)(2)).
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T2C03; 47 CFR 97.119(b)(2) (eCFR, current to 2026-09-22)

notes.front: What must a person have to be the control operator of a station transmitting in RACES?
notes.back: An FCC-issued amateur operator licence and certification by a civil defense organisation as enrolled in it.
notes.explanation: The station itself must also be certified as registered with a civil defense organisation (97.407(a)).
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: May a control operator ever transmit outside their licence class’s frequency privileges?
notes.back: Yes, but only in situations involving the immediate safety of human life or protection of property.
notes.explanation: 97.403 allows any means of radiocommunication for such needs when normal communication systems are not available.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T2C09; 47 CFR 97.403 (eCFR, current to 2026-09-22)

notes.front: On any frequency, to whom must every control operator give priority?
notes.back: To stations providing emergency communications, except those sending RACES training drills and tests.
notes.explanation: The rule is 97.101(c), and it applies at all times and on all frequencies.
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: When do the FCC Part 97 Amateur Radio Service rules NOT apply to the operation of an amateur station?
notes.back: FCC rules always apply
notes.choices:
A) When operating under RACES rules
B) When operating under FEMA rules
C) When operating under ARES rules
D) FCC rules always apply
notes.choicesExplained: A: RACES is itself a Part 97 service (97.3(a)(38)), so the rules apply. B: FEMA (the Federal Emergency Management Agency) rules do not suspend Part 97. C: ARES operation is still under Part 97.
notes.explanation: The pool keys “FCC rules always apply”; 97.103(a) makes the station licensee responsible for operating in accordance with the FCC Rules, with no exception for emergency groups.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T2C01; 47 CFR 97.103(a), 97.3(a)(38) (eCFR, current to 2026-09-22)

notes.front: Which of the following are typical duties of a Net Control Station?
notes.back: Call the net to order and direct communications between stations checking in
notes.choices:
A) Choose the regular net meeting time and frequency
B) Ensure that all stations checking into the net are properly licensed for operation on the net frequency
C) Call the net to order and direct communications between stations checking in
D) All these choices are correct
notes.choicesExplained: A: choosing the net's time and frequency is not among the duties the pool keys. B: the pool does not make the net control station check other stations' licences. D: “all” fails because A and B are not keyed.
notes.explanation: The net control station runs the net on the air: it calls the net to order and directs who transmits, which is why stations in a net transmit only when directed.

notes.front: What technique is used to ensure that voice messages containing unusual words are received correctly?
notes.back: Spell the words using a standard phonetic alphabet
notes.choices:
A) Send the words by voice and Morse code
B) Use the Q-code “QSR” to ask the receiving station to repeat the words back
C) Spell the words using a standard phonetic alphabet
D) All these choices are correct
notes.choicesExplained: A: sending in two modes is not the standard technique. B: QSR is not the keyed technique. D: only C is keyed.
notes.explanation: Unusual words are the ones most easily misheard; spelling them letter by letter in a standard phonetic alphabet removes the doubt. Part 97 encourages a phonetic alphabet for station identification too (97.119(b)(2)).
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T2C03; 47 CFR 97.119(b)(2) (eCFR, current to 2026-09-22)

notes.front: What is RACES?
notes.back: An FCC Part 97 amateur radio service for civil defense communications during national emergencies
notes.choices:
A) An emergency organization combining amateur radio and citizens band operators and frequencies
B) An international radio experimentation society
C) A radio contest held in a short period, sometimes called a “sprint”
D) An FCC Part 97 amateur radio service for civil defense communications during national emergencies
notes.choicesExplained: A: RACES uses amateur stations only, not citizens band. B: it is not an experimentation society. C: it is not a contest.
notes.explanation: RACES is a Part 97 service using amateur stations for civil defense communications; 97.3(a)(38) says during local, regional or national civil emergencies, so the pool's “national” is one case.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T2C04; 47 CFR 97.3(a)(38) (eCFR, current to 2026-09-22)

notes.front: What does the term “traffic” refer to in net operation?
notes.back: Formal messages exchanged by net stations
notes.choices:
A) Formal messages exchanged by net stations
B) The number of stations checking in and out of a net
C) Operation by mobile or portable stations
D) A count of the number of activations of the net each month
notes.choicesExplained: B: a count of check-ins is not traffic. C: mobile or portable operation is not traffic. D: a count of activations is not traffic.
notes.explanation: In net operation “traffic” means the messages themselves: formal messages passed between stations, with named parts such as the preamble and the check.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T2C05, T2C10, T2C11

notes.front: What is the Amateur Radio Emergency Service (ARES)?
notes.back: A group of licensed amateurs who have voluntarily registered their qualifications and equipment for communications duty in the public service
notes.choices:
A) A group of licensed amateurs who have voluntarily registered their qualifications and equipment for communications duty in the public service
B) A group of licensed amateurs who are members of the military and who voluntarily agreed to provide message handling services in the case of an emergency
C) A training program that provides licensing courses for those interested in obtaining an amateur license to use during emergencies
D) A training program that certifies amateur operators for membership in the Radio Amateur Civil Emergency Service
notes.choicesExplained: B: ARES members need not be military. C: ARES is not a licensing course. D: ARES does not certify operators for RACES; RACES needs civil defense certification.
notes.explanation: The key words are “voluntarily registered”: ARES members are licensed amateurs who have offered their qualifications and equipment for public service. RACES, by contrast, needs civil defense certification.

notes.front: Which of the following is standard practice when you participate in a net?
notes.back: Unless you are reporting an emergency, transmit only when directed by the net control station
notes.choices:
A) When first responding to the net control station, transmit your call sign, name, and address as in the FCC database
B) Record the time of each of your transmissions
C) Unless you are reporting an emergency, transmit only when directed by the net control station
D) All these choices are correct
notes.choicesExplained: A: you need not give your address when checking in. B: recording the time of each transmission is not the standard practice asked. D: only C is keyed.
notes.explanation: The net control station directs communications between the stations checking in, so you wait to be called; the one exception is reporting an emergency.

notes.front: Which of the following relays messages using email addresses based on amateur callsigns?
notes.back: Winlink
notes.choices:
A) Winlink
B) FT8
C) PSK31
D) AMTOR
notes.choicesExplained: B: FT8 is a digital mode, not an email relay system. C and D: PSK31 and AMTOR (Amateur Teleprinting Over Radio) are modes for sending text over the air, not a relay system built on call-sign email addresses.
notes.explanation: Winlink's addresses are built on amateur call signs, so messages can be relayed like email over amateur radio; the other choices are modes, not a messaging system.

notes.front: Are amateur station control operators ever permitted to operate outside the frequency privileges of their license class?
notes.back: Yes, but only in situations involving the immediate safety of human life or protection of property
notes.choices:
A) No
B) Yes, but only when part of a FEMA emergency plan
C) Yes, but only when part of a RACES emergency plan
D) Yes, but only in situations involving the immediate safety of human life or protection of property
notes.choicesExplained: A: there is an exception, so “no” is wrong. B: a FEMA (Federal Emergency Management Agency) plan does not create the exception. C: a RACES plan does not create the exception.
notes.explanation: Only for the immediate safety of human life or protection of property, when normal communications are unavailable (97.403).
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T2C09; 47 CFR 97.403 (eCFR, current to 2026-09-22)

notes.front: What information is contained in the preamble of a formal traffic message?
notes.back: Information needed to track the message
notes.choices:
A) The email address of the originating station
B) The address of the intended recipient
C) The telephone number of the addressee
D) Information needed to track the message
notes.choicesExplained: A: the originator’s email address is not the preamble. B: the addressee’s address is a separate part of the message. C: the addressee’s telephone number is a separate part of the message.
notes.explanation: The preamble carries what each station handling the message needs to keep track of it; the addressee's details are not part of it.

notes.front: What is meant by “check” in a radiogram header?
notes.back: The number of words or word equivalents in the text portion of the message
notes.choices:
A) The number of words or word equivalents in the text portion of the message
B) The call sign of the originating station
C) A list of stations that have relayed the message
D) A box on the message form that indicates that the message was received and/or relayed
notes.choicesExplained: B: the originator’s call sign is not the check. C: a relay list is not the check. D: the check is a count, not a received box.
notes.explanation: The check is a word count: the receiving station can count the words it copied and compare them with the check.

notes.front: Which of the following requires certification by a civil defense agency?
notes.back: RACES
notes.choices:
A) ARES
B) RACES
C) MARS
D) SKYWARN
notes.choicesExplained: A: ARES membership is voluntary registration, not civil defense certification. C: MARS (the Military Auxiliary Radio System) is not the service 97.407(a) ties to civil defense certification. D: SKYWARN is the National Weather Service's volunteer storm-spotter program, not a Part 97 service.
notes.explanation: 97.407(a) lets a station transmit in RACES only if it is certified as registered with a civil defense organisation, and its control operator certified as enrolled in one.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T2C12; 47 CFR 97.407(a) (eCFR, current to 2026-09-22); National Weather Service, “SKYWARN Storm Spotter Program” (weather.gov/skywarn)

notes.front: How does RACES differ from ARES?
notes.back: RACES is a Part 97 service for civil defense, needing civil defense certification; ARES is voluntary registration for public-service duty.
notes.explanation: Both serve in emergencies, and both operate under the FCC rules.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T2C04, T2C06, T2C12, T2C01
